Chapter 4: The Power and Limits of Language
You know, language is meant to help us connect—to help us really understand each other. But have you ever noticed how sometimes, the words we have just aren’t big enough for the lives we’re living? Especially for people whose experiences don’t fit the usual boxes. Folks who live at the edges, whose ways of loving or being don’t have neat labels—sometimes, the right words just... don’t exist.
In the early days of their relationship, our two partners find themselves stumbling over language. They talk about gender, about desire, about what it truly means to be together. But when it comes time to name their connection—boyfriend, girlfriend, husband, wife—none of those labels feel right. They feel borrowed, awkward, almost like they’re trying on someone else’s clothes.
So, they keep searching. Trying out different words, hoping something will finally feel true. But every term falls just a little bit short.
And it’s not just a personal struggle. It’s political, too. Our world loves categories—it’s built on the idea that everyone can be sorted into tidy little boxes. But for the people who don’t fit? Language becomes a battleground. Every word is a negotiation, a way of saying, “Hey, I deserve to exist on my own terms.”
The partners start reading, talking to friends, going to events—trying to figure it all out. And they discover something important: language is alive. It’s always shifting, always evolving. People invent new words, reclaim old ones. But even the best words can only stretch so far. There are always going to be gaps—things that just can’t be said.
Sometimes, when the words run out, the partners find comfort in silence. They learn to talk in other ways—maybe it’s a touch, a look, or just sharing a laugh. They realize that real intimacy isn’t just about what you say, but about being present, about being okay with the unknown. Most people want clear answers, want everything spelled out. But these two? They learn that not knowing is okay, too.
As their family grows, the dance with language gets even trickier. There are forms to fill out, questions from doctors and teachers, and chats with other parents. They have to decide, every time, how to describe themselves and their family. Sometimes, it’s just easier to go with the simplest answer, just to avoid a hassle. But other times, they stand their ground—even when it’s tough.
Over time, it becomes clear: language is both a tool and a trap. Sure, it helps us find each other, build community, make sense of our lives. But it can also limit, exclude, or even erase people’s experiences. The partners learn to use language carefully, and to be honest about what it can and can’t do. They know words will never be enough. But they also know that silence isn’t an option.
